prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
When you type an address such as https://www.example.com/products into a browser and press Enter, the browser first works out what you have given it. It splits the string into a scheme (https), a host (www.example.com), an optional port and a path. Because the scheme is https, the port defaults to 443. The browser also checks whether the host is on its HSTS list, which records sites that must only be reached over HTTPS. If you had typed http:// for such a site, the browser would rewrite the address itself rather than make a plain request first.

Next the browser looks for a reason not to use the network. If a service worker is registered for the origin, it gets the chance to answer the request. Otherwise the HTTP cache is checked. A stored copy that is still fresh, according to its Cache-Control max-age or Expires header, is used directly and no request is sent. A stale copy may be revalidated with a conditional request, using an ETag or Last-Modified value, and that still needs a connection and the steps below. The browser also looks for an already open connection to the same origin, and if one exists it skips straight to sending the request.

If a new connection is needed, the browser needs an IP address for the host. It asks its own DNS cache, then the operating system's cache and the hosts file. If none of them has an answer, the operating system sends a query to a recursive resolver, usually run by the internet provider or a public service such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. The resolver has its own cache, and for a popular name it often holds the answer already. If not, it asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks one of those which servers are responsible for example.com, and asks one of those for the records of www.example.com. The answer is an A record holding an IPv4 address, an AAAA record holding an IPv6 address, or both, and each carries a time to live in seconds that says how long it may be cached. A lookup answered from a cache takes a millisecond or so. One that goes the full way can take 50 to 200 milliseconds. Browsers now also ask for an HTTPS record, which can tell them the server supports HTTP/3.

With an address in hand, the browser opens a connection. For HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 this is TCP. The client sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the client answers with an ACK. The client can send data as soon as it sends that ACK, so the handshake costs one round trip time. A round trip to a server on the same continent is commonly 20 to 80 milliseconds, and across an ocean it is more like 100 to 150. Where the browser already knows the server speaks HTTP/3, from a previous visit's Alt-Svc header or from the HTTPS record, it can use QUIC over UDP instead. QUIC combines the transport set-up and the encryption set-up into a single exchange.

Over TCP, TLS comes next. In TLS 1.3 the client sends a ClientHello containing the versions and cipher suites it supports, a random value, a key share for an elliptic curve exchange such as X25519, the server name in the SNI field, and the protocols it can speak in the ALPN field, normally h2 and http/1.1. The server picks a cipher suite and replies with its own key share. From the two key shares both sides derive the same secret, and everything the server sends after its ServerHello is encrypted. That includes its certificate chain, a signature proving it holds the private key that matches the certificate, and a Finished message. The client then checks the certificate. It confirms that the chain leads to a root authority in its trust store, that the dates are valid, that the name www.example.com appears in the certificate's subject alternative names, and, depending on the browser, that the certificate has not been revoked. If any check fails, the browser shows a warning page and sends nothing. Otherwise the client sends its own Finished message, and application data can flow. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip, where TLS 1.2 needed two. If the browser has visited before and holds a session ticket, it can resume the session and in some cases send the request in its first flight as early data. Early data can be replayed by an attacker, so it is limited to requests that are safe to repeat.

ALPN settles which HTTP version is used. With h2 the browser sends the request as a set of frames on a stream. The request is a method, GET, a path, /products, and headers: the :authority pseudo-header with the host name, accept, accept-encoding listing gzip and br, user-agent, and any cookies stored for the domain. HTTP/2 compresses these headers with HPACK, so a repeated request on the same connection is much smaller than the first. HTTP/1.1 sends the same information as lines of text inside the encrypted channel.

The request crosses the network and reaches the server's edge, which is often a CDN or load balancer instead of the machine that holds the application. That edge ends the TLS session, and it may have the response in its cache and reply at once. If not, it forwards the request to an origin server, perhaps over a connection it already keeps open. The application routes /products to a handler, which may read from a database, build the page, and set a 200 status code and headers such as Content-Type and Cache-Control. The server can start sending as soon as the status line and headers are ready, without waiting for the whole body. The first byte of that reply reaching the browser is what tools report as time to first byte.

Adding up the steps for a first visit to a distant server over TCP and TLS 1.3, there is a DNS lookup, one round trip for TCP, one for TLS, and one for the request and the start of the response, plus the time the server spends working. With a 50 millisecond round trip and a 40 millisecond DNS lookup, the network alone accounts for about 190 milliseconds before any application code is counted. A second visit may skip DNS, reuse the connection, and be served from cache, which is why the same address can feel quick on one visit and slow on another. The parts a developer usually controls are the server's processing time, whether a CDN sits in front of it, the cache headers, and whether HTTP/3 and TLS 1.3 are enabled. The rest is set by distance and by the number of round trips.
